questions.question_text: Under section 2(20) of the Companies Act, 2013, the term 'company' means:

options.A: A company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 only
options.B: A company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 or under any previous company law
options.C: Any body corporate, whether incorporated in India or outside India
options.D: Any association of persons carrying on business for profit and registered with the Registrar

questions.explanation: Section 2(20) defines 'company' as a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 or under any previous company law. A body corporate (section 2(11)) is a wider term and includes a company incorporated outside India. Companies registered under earlier Acts such as the Companies Act, 1956 are also 'companies'.

questions.question_text: Kaveri Tools Private Limited has the following members: 170 individuals who are neither present nor past employees (this figure includes 6 pairs of joint holders), 20 current employees who hold shares, and 9 former employees who became members while in employment and continue as members. For the limit on members in section 2(68), how many members are counted?
questions.explanation: Under section 2(68), employee-members and former employees who became members while in employment and continue to be members are excluded from the 200 limit. Joint holders are treated as a single member. Of the 170 non-employee members, 12 persons form 6 joint holdings, so they count as 6 rather than 12: 170 - 12 + 6 = 164. The 20 employees and 9 former employees are ignored.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a restriction that the articles of a private company must contain under section 2(68)?

options.A: A prohibition on any invitation to the public to subscribe for its securities
options.B: A restriction on the company accepting loans from its directors
options.C: A restriction on the right to transfer its shares
options.D: A limit on the number of its members to two hundred, except in the case of a One Person Company

questions.explanation: Section 2(68) requires the articles of a private company to restrict the right to transfer shares, limit the number of members to 200 (except an OPC) and prohibit any invitation to the public to subscribe for its securities. The Act places no such restriction on accepting loans from directors.

questions.question_text: Megha Ltd is a subsidiary of Trident Ltd, a public company. The articles of Megha Ltd contain all the restrictions applicable to a private company. Megha Ltd will be treated as:

options.A: A private company, because its articles contain the restrictions of section 2(68)
options.B: Neither a private nor a public company, but a deemed foreign company
options.C: A private company, unless the Central Government declares it to be public
options.D: A public company, because a subsidiary of a public company is deemed to be a public company

questions.explanation: The proviso to section 2(71) states that a company which is a subsidiary of a company that is not a private company is deemed to be a public company for the purposes of the Act. This applies even if the subsidiary's articles keep the restrictions of a private company.

questions.question_text: As per section 2(87), Company X will be a subsidiary of Company Y if Company Y:

options.A: Exercises or controls more than one-half of the total voting power of Company X, either on its own or together with its subsidiaries
options.B: Is a major supplier of raw material to Company X under a long-term contract
options.C: Has significant influence over Company X through holding 20% of its voting power
options.D: Holds exactly one-half of the total share capital of Company X

questions.explanation: Under section 2(87), a holding company either controls the composition of the board of directors of the other company, or exercises or controls more than one-half of its total voting power. This can be on its own or together with one or more of its subsidiaries. Significant influence through 20% of voting power makes a company an associate under section 2(6), not a subsidiary. Exactly one-half is not 'more than one-half'.

questions.question_text: Under the Explanation to section 2(6), 'significant influence' for identifying an associate company means control of at least ______ of the total voting power, or control of or participation in business decisions under an agreement.

options.A: Ten per cent
options.B: More than fifty per cent
options.C: Twenty-six per cent
options.D: Twenty per cent

questions.explanation: The Explanation to section 2(6) defines significant influence as control of at least 20% of the total voting power, or control of or participation in business decisions under an agreement. An associate company also includes a joint venture company.

questions.question_text: Which of the following companies can be a 'small company' under section 2(85), provided it meets the capital and turnover criteria?

options.A: A private company that is neither a holding nor a subsidiary company
options.B: A company registered under section 8
options.C: A company governed by a special Act
options.D: A private company that is a subsidiary of another private company

questions.explanation: Section 2(85) excludes a holding company, a subsidiary company, a company registered under section 8 and a company or body corporate governed by any special Act. A small company must also be a company other than a public company. A standalone private company within the prescribed limits qualifies.

questions.question_text: As per section 2(51), which of the following is NOT automatically a Key Managerial Personnel?

options.A: The Company Secretary
options.B: A general manager two levels below the directors
options.C: The Chief Financial Officer
options.D: A whole-time director

questions.explanation: Key managerial personnel under section 2(51) are the CEO, managing director or manager, the company secretary, the whole-time director and the CFO. The board may also designate an officer in whole-time employment who is not more than one level below the directors. An officer two levels below the directors cannot be designated, so the general manager is not a KMP.

questions.question_text: Mr. Arjun is a director of Sunrise Ltd. Which of the following is a 'related party' of Sunrise Ltd under section 2(76)?

options.A: A public company in which Mr. Arjun holds 3% of the shares but is not a director
options.B: A private company in which Mr. Arjun's brother is a member
options.C: A firm in which Mr. Arjun's cousin is a partner
options.D: A public company in which Mr. Arjun is a director and, together with his relatives, holds 1.5% of the paid-up share capital

questions.explanation: Section 2(76) includes a private company in which a director or manager, or his relative, is a member or director. A brother is a relative under section 2(77) and the related rules. A public company is related only if the director or manager is a director of it AND holds, with relatives, more than 2% of its paid-up capital. A cousin is not a relative under the Act.

questions.topic: Incorporation of Company and Matters Incidental Thereto
questions.question_text: Under section 3(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, the minimum number of persons required to form a public company, a private company and a One Person Company respectively is:

options.A: Seven, two and one
options.B: Two, seven and one
options.C: Five, two and one
options.D: Seven, two and two

questions.explanation: Section 3(1) allows a company to be formed for a lawful purpose by seven or more persons for a public company, two or more persons for a private company, and one person for a One Person Company. Each must subscribe to the memorandum and complete registration.

questions.topic: Incorporation of Company and Matters Incidental Thereto
questions.question_text: Pioneer Ltd, a public company, has had only five members for the last ten months and continues to carry on business. Under section 3A, Mr. Rao, a member who knows this, is:

options.A: Severally liable for the payment of the whole of the debts contracted during the period after the first six months
options.B: Liable only to the extent of the amount unpaid on his shares
options.C: Liable for all the company's debts, including debts contracted before membership fell below seven
options.D: Not personally liable at all, because the members' liability is limited

questions.explanation: Section 3A applies where a public company's membership falls below seven, or a private company's below two, and the company carries on business for more than six months while so reduced. Every person who is a member during the period after those six months, and knows of it, is severally liable for the whole of the debts contracted during that period. He may be sued for them. The liability does not reach debts contracted earlier.

questions.topic: Incorporation of Company and Matters Incidental Thereto
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a clause required to be stated in the memorandum of a company limited by shares under section 4?

options.A: The objects clause
options.B: The procedure for transfer of shares
options.C: The name clause
options.D: The liability clause

questions.explanation: Section 4 requires the memorandum to state the name, the State of the registered office, the objects, the liability of members, the capital (for a company with share capital) and the subscribers. For an OPC it must also state the nominee. The procedure for transfer of shares is a matter for the articles, not the memorandum.

questions.topic: Incorporation of Company and Matters Incidental Thereto
questions.question_text: Under section 5(3) and (4), entrenchment provisions can be included in the articles of a public company:

options.A: Only with the prior approval of the Tribunal
options.B: Only on formation, or by an amendment agreed to by all the members
options.C: Only on formation, or by an amendment agreed to by special resolution
options.D: Only by an ordinary resolution followed by approval of the Registrar

questions.explanation: Section 5(3) allows the articles to contain entrenchment provisions, under which specified provisions can be altered only if conditions more restrictive than a special resolution are met. Under section 5(4) they may be made on formation or by an amendment. In a private company the amendment needs the agreement of all members; in a public company it needs a special resolution.

questions.topic: Incorporation of Company and Matters Incidental Thereto
questions.question_text: As per section 7(2), the certificate of incorporation issued by the Registrar is:

options.A: Valid only after the company files its declaration for commencement of business
options.B: Evidence that the objects of the company are lawful in all respects
options.C: Conclusive evidence that all the requirements of the Act regarding registration have been complied with
options.D: Prima facie evidence only, which can be rebutted by any member

questions.explanation: Section 7(2) provides that the certificate of incorporation is conclusive evidence that all the requirements of the Act regarding registration and matters precedent and incidental to it have been complied with. Its validity does not depend on the later declaration under section 10A.

questions.topic: Incorporation of Company and Matters Incidental Thereto
questions.question_text: Under section 10A, a company with share capital that was incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 must file a declaration that every subscriber has paid the value of the shares agreed to be taken. This declaration must be filed within:

options.A: 90 days of the date of incorporation
options.B: 180 days of the date of incorporation
options.C: 30 days of the date of incorporation
options.D: One year of the date of incorporation

questions.explanation: Section 10A(1) provides that such a company shall not commence business or exercise borrowing powers unless a director files a declaration within 180 days of incorporation. The declaration confirms that every subscriber to the memorandum has paid the value of the shares agreed to be taken. The company must also verify its registered office under section 12(2).

questions.topic: Incorporation of Company and Matters Incidental Thereto
questions.question_text: Which of the following purposes does NOT qualify a company for a licence under section 8?

options.A: Promotion of education and research
options.B: Protection of the environment
options.C: Promotion of sports
options.D: Distribution of profits to members by way of dividend

questions.explanation: Section 8 applies to a company formed to promote commerce, art, science, sports, education, research, social welfare, religion, charity, protection of the environment or similar objects. It must apply its profits or income to promoting those objects, and its articles must prohibit the payment of dividend to members.

questions.topic: Incorporation of Company and Matters Incidental Thereto
questions.question_text: Bright Ltd wants to shift its registered office from Pune (Maharashtra) to Bengaluru (Karnataka). Under section 13, in addition to a special resolution, the alteration of its memorandum requires the approval of:

options.A: The Registrar of Companies of Maharashtra only
options.B: The Tribunal
options.C: The Central Government
options.D: The Securities and Exchange Board of India

questions.explanation: Under section 13(4), an alteration of the memorandum to shift the registered office from one State to another needs a special resolution and the approval of the Central Government. That power has been delegated to the Regional Director. A shift within the same State but outside the jurisdiction of the existing Registrar is dealt with under section 12.

questions.topic: Incorporation of Company and Matters Incidental Thereto
questions.question_text: The articles of Zenith Ltd require that any borrowing above a stated limit be approved by an ordinary resolution of members. The directors borrowed above the limit without a resolution. A lender who had no knowledge of the omission wishes to enforce the loan. Which doctrine protects the lender?

options.A: The doctrine of indoor management
options.B: The doctrine of ultra vires
options.C: The doctrine of lifting the corporate veil
options.D: The doctrine of constructive notice

questions.explanation: The doctrine of indoor management, from Royal British Bank v. Turquand, lets an outsider dealing in good faith assume that internal procedures such as passing a members' resolution have been followed. Constructive notice works against outsiders, but only for the contents of public documents, not whether internal steps were taken. Protection is lost where the outsider knew of the irregularity, was negligent, or the act was a forgery.

questions.topic: Incorporation of Company and Matters Incidental Thereto
questions.question_text: Ruby Ltd entered into a contract that is beyond the objects stated in its memorandum. At the next general meeting, all members unanimously resolved to ratify the contract. The legal position of the contract is that it:

options.A: Remains void and cannot be ratified even by the unanimous consent of all members
options.B: Becomes valid from the date of the resolution
options.C: Becomes valid only if the Registrar approves the ratification
options.D: Becomes valid from the date of the contract, since ratification relates back

questions.explanation: Under the doctrine of ultra vires, settled in Ashbury Railway Carriage and Iron Co. Ltd v. Riche, an act beyond the objects of the memorandum is void ab initio. It cannot be ratified even by all the members, because the company never had the capacity to do it. An act ultra vires the directors but intra vires the company can be ratified by members.

questions.topic: Incorporation of Company and Matters Incidental Thereto
questions.question_text: Under section 12(1), a company must have a registered office capable of receiving and acknowledging all communications and notices addressed to it:

options.A: Within six months of its incorporation
options.B: Before applying for incorporation
options.C: Within thirty days of its incorporation and at all times thereafter
options.D: Only after it commences business under section 10A

questions.explanation: Section 12(1) requires every company, within thirty days of incorporation and at all times thereafter, to have a registered office capable of receiving and acknowledging all communications and notices. Verification of the registered office is filed with the Registrar within the same period.

questions.question_text: Under section 23(1), a public company may issue securities to the public:

options.A: Only through a rights issue
options.B: Through a prospectus
options.C: Only through private placement
options.D: Only through bonus issue

questions.explanation: Section 23(1) states that a public company may issue securities to the public through a prospectus. It may also issue them through private placement, by way of a rights issue or a bonus issue. Section 23(2) allows a private company to issue securities only by rights issue, bonus issue or private placement.

questions.question_text: Section 25 deems a document containing an offer for sale of securities to the public to be a prospectus issued by the company. Unless the contrary is proved, an allotment with a view to the securities being offered for sale to the public is presumed where:

options.A: The securities are listed on a recognised stock exchange
options.B: The offer for sale is made within one year after the allotment
options.C: The allottee is a director of the company
options.D: The offer for sale is made within six months after the allotment, or before the whole consideration for the securities has been received by the company

questions.explanation: Section 25(2) presumes that an allotment was made with a view to an offer for sale to the public in either of two cases. The first is that the offer was made within six months after the allotment. The second is that, at the date of the offer, the whole consideration had not been received by the company. The document is then a deemed prospectus.

questions.question_text: A red herring prospectus under section 32 is a prospectus that:

options.A: Is valid for one year and covers multiple issues
options.B: Does not include complete particulars of the quantum or price of the securities included in it
options.C: Contains a false statement and is liable to be cancelled
options.D: Is issued only by a company incorporated outside India

questions.explanation: As per the Explanation to section 32, a red herring prospectus does not include complete particulars of the quantum or price of the securities. Once the offer closes, the prospectus stating the total capital raised, the closing price and any details left out must be filed with the Registrar and SEBI. A prospectus covering several issues over a period is a shelf prospectus under section 31.

questions.question_text: As per section 31, a shelf prospectus is valid for a period not exceeding:

options.A: Ninety days from the date of filing with the Registrar
options.B: One year from the date of opening of the first offer of securities under it
options.C: Three years from the date of its issue
options.D: Six months from the date of filing with the Registrar

questions.explanation: Section 31(1) allows prescribed classes of companies to file a shelf prospectus. Under it, no further prospectus is needed for subsequent offers within a period of validity not exceeding one year from the date of opening of the first offer. An information memorandum must be filed before each subsequent offer.

questions.question_text: Which of the following persons is NOT liable to pay compensation under section 35 for a misleading statement in a prospectus?

options.A: A person who authorised the issue of the prospectus
options.B: A person who withdrew his consent to act as director before the issue of the prospectus, and the prospectus was issued without his authority
options.C: A promoter of the company who knew about the misleading statement
options.D: A person named in the prospectus as a proposed director with his consent

questions.explanation: Section 35(1) makes directors, persons named with their consent as proposed directors, promoters, persons who authorised the issue and experts liable to compensate those who subscribed on the faith of a misleading prospectus. Section 35(2) excuses a person who, having consented to become a director, withdrew that consent before the issue, and the prospectus was issued without his authority or consent.

questions.question_text: Under section 39(2), the amount payable on application on every security offered in a public issue shall not be less than:

options.A: The full nominal amount of the security
options.B: Twenty-five per cent of the issue price of the security
options.C: Ten per cent of the nominal amount of the security
options.D: Five per cent of the nominal amount of the security, or such other percentage or amount as SEBI may specify

questions.explanation: Section 39(2) provides that the amount payable on application on every security shall not be less than five per cent of its nominal amount, or such other percentage or amount as SEBI may specify by regulations. SEBI regulations for listed issues prescribe higher application money.

questions.question_text: Under section 39(3), if the stated minimum amount has not been subscribed and the sums payable on application have not been received within thirty days from the date of issue of the prospectus, or such other period as SEBI may specify:

options.A: The company may allot shares in proportion to the money received
options.B: The directors must subscribe for the shortfall
options.C: The application money must be returned within the prescribed period
options.D: The company must issue a fresh prospectus within thirty days

questions.explanation: Section 39(1) prohibits allotment unless the minimum amount stated in the prospectus has been subscribed and the application money received. Under section 39(3), if this does not happen within thirty days of the issue of the prospectus, or the period specified by SEBI, the amount received must be returned within the prescribed time.

questions.question_text: Nova Pvt Ltd received application money in a private placement on 1 June. It has not allotted the securities. Under section 42(6), which of the following is correct?

options.A: It must allot within 90 days of receipt; if not, refund with interest at 15% per annum from the date of receipt
options.B: It must allot within 60 days of receipt; if not, refund within 15 days after the 60 days, failing which it pays interest at 12% per annum from the expiry of the 60th day
options.C: It must allot within 30 days of receipt, failing which the money becomes a deposit immediately
options.D: It must allot within 60 days of receipt; if not, refund within 30 days after the 60 days without any interest

questions.explanation: Section 42(6) requires a company making a private placement to allot within sixty days from receipt of the application money. If it cannot, it must repay the money within fifteen days from the end of the sixty days. If it fails to repay within that time, it must repay with interest at twelve per cent per annum from the expiry of the sixtieth day.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT permitted for a private placement under section 42?

options.A: Releasing a public advertisement about the offer through newspapers
options.B: Making an offer to qualified institutional buyers in addition to other identified persons
options.C: Receiving subscription money by cheque from identified persons
options.D: Issuing a private placement offer and application letter to identified persons

questions.explanation: Section 42(7) prohibits a company making a private placement from releasing any public advertisement, or using any media, marketing or distribution channel or agent, to inform the public about the offer. Under section 42(4), subscription money must be paid by cheque, demand draft or other banking channel, not in cash. Offers to qualified institutional buyers are permitted.

questions.question_text: Under section 34, a person who authorises the issue of a prospectus containing an untrue or misleading statement is liable to action under:

options.A: Section 36, which deals only with misleading advertisements
options.B: Section 35, which deals only with civil liability
options.C: The Indian Contract Act, 1872 only
options.D: Section 447, which deals with punishment for fraud

questions.explanation: Section 34 provides that where a prospectus includes any untrue or misleading statement, or omits a matter likely to mislead, every person who authorises its issue is liable under section 447 (fraud). It is a defence to prove that the statement or omission was immaterial, or that he had reasonable grounds to believe it was true. Section 35 deals with civil liability separately.

questions.question_text: Under section 43, the share capital of a company limited by shares can be of which kinds?

options.A: Authorised, issued and reserve share capital
options.B: Equity share capital (with voting rights or with differential rights) and preference share capital
options.C: Equity share capital only
options.D: Equity share capital, preference share capital and deferred share capital

questions.explanation: Section 43 provides for two kinds of share capital: equity share capital and preference share capital. Equity share capital may carry voting rights or differential rights as to dividend, voting or otherwise, in accordance with the rules.

questions.question_text: Under section 47(2), preference shareholders of a class become entitled to vote on every resolution placed before the company when the dividend on that class has remained unpaid for a period of:

options.A: Three years or more
options.B: Five years or more
options.C: One year or more
options.D: Two years or more

questions.explanation: Normally, under section 47(2), preference shareholders vote only on resolutions that directly affect their rights, such as winding up or the repayment or reduction of capital. If dividend on a class of preference shares has not been paid for two years or more, that class may vote on all resolutions.

questions.question_text: The rights of a class of shareholders are varied under section 48 with the written consent of the holders of 80% of the issued shares of that class. Holders of 12% of that class did not consent. What remedy do they have?

options.A: None, because the variation was approved by holders of more than three-fourths
options.B: They may apply to the Tribunal to have the variation cancelled, as they hold not less than 10% of the issued shares of that class
options.C: They may apply to the Central Government, since only holders of 25% can approach the Tribunal
options.D: They may require the company to buy back their shares at fair value

questions.explanation: Section 48(1) allows variation of class rights with the written consent of holders of not less than three-fourths of the issued shares of that class, or by a special resolution passed at a separate class meeting. Under section 48(2), holders of not less than ten per cent of the issued shares of the class who did not consent may apply to the Tribunal to cancel the variation. The variation then has effect only if the Tribunal confirms it.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a permitted use of the securities premium account under section 52(2)?

options.A: Payment of dividend to equity shareholders
options.B: Writing off preliminary expenses of the company
options.C: Providing for the premium payable on redemption of debentures
options.D: Issuing unissued shares to members as fully paid bonus shares

questions.explanation: Section 52(2) permits the securities premium account to be used for fully paid bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, writing off expenses, commission or discount on the issue of shares or debentures, the premium payable on redemption of preference shares or debentures, and buy-back under section 68. It is treated like paid-up share capital, so it cannot be used to pay dividend.

questions.question_text: Under section 53, any share issued by a company at a discount is void. The only exceptions are sweat equity shares under section 54 and:

options.A: Shares issued to promoters in a rights issue
options.B: Shares issued to the public in a fresh issue below par to attract investors
options.C: Shares issued to creditors on conversion of debt under a statutory restructuring scheme or arrangement under RBI guidelines
options.D: Bonus shares issued out of free reserves

questions.explanation: Section 53(1) prohibits issuing shares at a discount and section 53(2) makes such shares void, except sweat equity shares under section 54. Section 53(2A) further permits a company to issue shares at a discount to its creditors when debt is converted into shares under a statutory resolution plan or a debt restructuring scheme under RBI guidelines.

questions.question_text: Delta Ltd redeems fully paid preference shares of nominal value ₹8,00,000 at par. It uses ₹3,00,000 raised from a fresh issue of equity shares at par made for the purpose, and pays the rest out of profits available for dividend. What amount must be transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve under section 55?
questions.explanation: Under section 55(2), when preference shares are redeemed out of profits, a sum equal to the nominal amount of the shares redeemed out of profits must be transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve. Shares redeemed from a fresh issue need no transfer. Nominal value redeemed out of profits = ₹8,00,000 - ₹3,00,000 = ₹5,00,000.

questions.question_text: Under section 55, a company limited by shares cannot issue preference shares that are:

options.A: Cumulative
options.B: Convertible into equity shares
options.C: Participating
options.D: Irredeemable

questions.explanation: Section 55(1) states that no company limited by shares shall issue any preference shares that are irredeemable. Preference shares must generally be redeemed within twenty years from the date of issue. A longer period is allowed for prescribed infrastructure projects, subject to annual redemption of a portion at the option of the holders.

questions.question_text: Under section 62(1)(a), when a company offers further shares to existing equity shareholders by a rights issue, the offer must be open for a period of:

options.A: Exactly twenty-one days from the date of the offer
options.B: Not less than thirty days and not exceeding sixty days
options.C: Not less than fifteen days and not exceeding thirty days from the date of the offer
options.D: Not less than seven days and not exceeding fifteen days

questions.explanation: Section 62(1)(a)(i) requires the offer to be made by notice specifying the number of shares offered. It must allow a period of not less than fifteen days and not exceeding thirty days from the date of the offer, after which an offer not accepted is deemed declined.

questions.question_text: Orbit Ltd has: free reserves ₹40 lakh, securities premium ₹15 lakh, capital redemption reserve ₹10 lakh and revaluation reserve ₹25 lakh. What is the maximum amount it can capitalise for fully paid bonus shares under section 63?

options.A: ₹55 lakh
options.B: ₹90 lakh
options.C: ₹40 lakh
options.D: ₹65 lakh

questions.explanation: Section 63(1) permits bonus shares to be issued only out of free reserves, the securities premium account and the capital redemption reserve account. The proviso to section 63(1) bars capitalising reserves created by revaluation of assets. Maximum = 40 + 15 + 10 = ₹65 lakh.

questions.question_text: Crest Ltd has paid-up equity share capital of ₹40 crore, a general reserve (free reserve) of ₹25 crore and a securities premium account of ₹15 crore. What is the maximum buy-back the Board can approve under section 68 without a special resolution of members?

options.A: ₹20 crore
options.B: ₹4 crore
options.C: ₹6.5 crore
options.D: ₹8 crore

questions.explanation: Under the proviso to section 68(2)(b), the Board may authorise a buy-back of up to ten per cent of the total paid-up equity capital and free reserves. Under the Explanation to section 68, free reserves include the securities premium account. Base = 40 + 25 + 15 = ₹80 crore, so the Board limit = 10% x 80 = ₹8 crore. A larger buy-back, up to 25%, needs a special resolution.

questions.question_text: Under section 56(4), unless prohibited by any law or court order, every company must deliver the certificates in respect of debentures allotted within:

options.A: Six months from the date of allotment
options.B: Two months from the date of allotment
options.C: Thirty days from the date of allotment
options.D: One month from the date of allotment

questions.explanation: Section 56(4) sets the time limits for delivering certificates. For subscribers to the memorandum it is two months from incorporation. For any allotment of shares it is two months from allotment. For a transfer or transmission it is one month from receipt of the instrument of transfer or intimation. For debentures it is six months from allotment.

questions.topic: Acceptance of Deposits by Companies and Registration of Charges
questions.question_text: Silverline Ltd, a public company, received the following sums. Which one is a 'deposit' under section 2(31) read with the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014?

options.A: An amount received from the Central Government
options.B: A loan from a scheduled commercial bank
options.C: An inter-corporate loan from another company
options.D: An unsecured loan from the wife of one of its directors

questions.explanation: Section 2(31) treats any receipt of money by way of deposit or loan as a deposit, except categories excluded by the rules. Amounts from the Central or State Government, banking companies and other companies are excluded. A loan from a director is excluded, and a loan from a relative of a director is excluded only for a private company. A loan from a director's relative to a public company is therefore a deposit.

questions.topic: Acceptance of Deposits by Companies and Registration of Charges
questions.question_text: Harbour Ltd accepts deposits from its members under section 73(2). Its deposits maturing during the next financial year total ₹2.5 crore. By 30 April, what is the minimum amount it must place in a deposit repayment reserve account?

options.A: ₹62.5 lakh
options.B: ₹25 lakh
options.C: ₹2.5 crore
options.D: ₹50 lakh

questions.explanation: Section 73(2)(c) requires a company accepting deposits from members to deposit, on or before 30 April each year, at least twenty per cent of the deposits maturing during the following financial year. The money is kept in a separate account with a scheduled bank called the deposit repayment reserve account. 20% x ₹2.5 crore = ₹50 lakh.

questions.topic: Acceptance of Deposits by Companies and Registration of Charges
questions.question_text: Under section 73(1), the provisions of Chapter V on acceptance of deposits do NOT apply to:

options.A: A private company with share capital
options.B: A listed public company that is not a financial institution
options.C: A banking company
options.D: A company registered under section 8

questions.explanation: Section 73(1) provides that the provisions of Chapter V do not apply to a banking company, a non-banking financial company as defined in the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, a housing finance company registered with the National Housing Bank, and other notified companies. Such entities are governed by their own regulators.

questions.topic: Acceptance of Deposits by Companies and Registration of Charges
questions.question_text: A company accepted deposits with intent to defraud the depositors. Under section 75, every officer of the company responsible for accepting such deposits is:

options.A: Not liable, as the deposits are the liability of the company alone
options.B: Liable only if the Registrar has issued a prior show-cause notice
options.C: Personally responsible, without any limitation of liability, for all or any of the losses or damages incurred by the depositors
options.D: Liable only up to the amount of his own shareholding

questions.explanation: Section 75(1) provides that where a company fails to repay a deposit and it is proved that the deposit was accepted with intent to defraud, or for a fraudulent purpose, the officers responsible are liable. Every officer responsible for the acceptance is personally responsible, without limitation of liability, for the depositors' losses, in addition to liability under section 447.

questions.topic: Acceptance of Deposits by Companies and Registration of Charges
questions.question_text: Share application money received by a company becomes a 'deposit' under the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014 if the securities are not allotted within sixty days of receipt and the money is not refunded within:

options.A: Fifteen days from the date of completion of the sixty days
options.B: Seven days from the date of completion of the sixty days
options.C: Thirty days from the date of completion of the sixty days
options.D: Ninety days from the date of receipt of the money

questions.explanation: Under the rules, share application money received for allotment is not a deposit. However, if the securities are not allotted within sixty days of receipt and the money is not refunded within fifteen days after that, the money is treated as a deposit. The approach mirrors section 42(6) on private placement.

questions.topic: Acceptance of Deposits by Companies and Registration of Charges
questions.question_text: Under section 77(1), it is the duty of every company creating a charge to register its particulars with the Registrar within:

options.A: Seven days of its creation
options.B: Ninety days of its creation
options.C: Thirty days of its creation
options.D: Sixty days of its creation

questions.explanation: Section 77(1) requires every company creating a charge within or outside India, on its property or assets or any of its undertakings, to register the particulars of the charge with the Registrar within thirty days of its creation. The Registrar may allow registration within extended periods under the provisos on payment of additional fees.

questions.topic: Acceptance of Deposits by Companies and Registration of Charges
questions.question_text: Peak Ltd borrowed ₹50 lakh from a bank against a charge on its machinery but never registered the charge. Peak Ltd later went into liquidation. Which of the following is correct?

options.A: The directors become personally liable to repay the entire loan to the bank
options.B: The charge is not taken into account by the liquidator, but the bank can still prove for the ₹50 lakh as an unsecured creditor
options.C: The charge is valid against the liquidator since the bank has the original charge document
options.D: The loan itself becomes void and the bank cannot recover any amount

questions.explanation: Under section 77(3), a charge is not taken into account by the liquidator or any creditor unless it has been registered and a certificate of registration issued. Section 77(4) adds that this does not prejudice any contract or obligation for repayment of the money secured. The bank loses its security but the debt survives, so it ranks as an unsecured creditor.

questions.topic: Acceptance of Deposits by Companies and Registration of Charges
questions.question_text: Where a company fails to register a charge within the time allowed, the charge-holder may apply to the Registrar under section 78. The Registrar may allow registration if the company does not register the charge, or show sufficient cause against registration, within:

options.A: Fourteen days after the Registrar gives notice to the company
options.B: Sixty days after the creation of the charge
options.C: Thirty days after the Registrar gives notice to the company
options.D: Seven days after the charge-holder's application

questions.explanation: Section 78 allows the person in whose favour the charge is created to apply for registration. Within fourteen days after giving notice to the company, the Registrar may allow registration unless the company itself registers the charge or shows sufficient cause why it should not be registered.

questions.topic: Acceptance of Deposits by Companies and Registration of Charges
questions.question_text: Under section 82(1), a company must inform the Registrar of the payment or satisfaction in full of any registered charge within:

options.A: Sixty days from the date of such payment or satisfaction
options.B: Thirty days from the date of such payment or satisfaction
options.C: The date of the next annual general meeting
options.D: Fourteen days from the date of such payment or satisfaction

questions.explanation: Section 82(1) requires the company to give intimation of the payment or satisfaction in full of a registered charge within thirty days in the prescribed form. The Registrar then issues a notice to the charge-holder to show cause why the satisfaction should not be recorded.

questions.topic: Acceptance of Deposits by Companies and Registration of Charges
questions.question_text: As per section 80, a person acquiring property of a company on which a charge has been registered under section 77 is deemed to have notice of the charge:

options.A: From the date the charge was created, whether registered or not
options.B: Only if the company informs him in writing
options.C: Only after the charge is entered in the company's own register of charges
options.D: From the date of such registration

questions.explanation: Section 80 states that where a charge on any property or assets of a company or its undertakings is registered under section 77, any person acquiring that property or any part of it shall be deemed to have notice of the charge from the date of such registration. Registration therefore operates as constructive notice to the world.

questions.question_text: Under section 91, a company may close its register of members, after giving at least seven days' notice, for periods aggregating not more than ______ in a year, and not more than ______ at any one time.

options.A: Sixty days; forty-five days
options.B: Forty-five days; twenty-one days
options.C: Thirty days; fifteen days
options.D: Forty-five days; thirty days

questions.explanation: Section 91(1) permits a company to close its register of members or debenture-holders or other security holders for any period or periods not exceeding forty-five days in the aggregate in a year. No single closure may exceed thirty days, and at least seven days' prior notice is required.

questions.question_text: Under section 92(4), a company must file its annual return with the Registrar within:

options.A: Sixty days from the date on which the annual general meeting is held, or from the date on which it should have been held
options.B: Thirty days from the date of the annual general meeting
options.C: Thirty days from the date of the board meeting approving the financial statements
options.D: Six months from the close of the financial year

questions.explanation: Section 92(4) requires every company to file a copy of the annual return with the Registrar within sixty days from the date on which the annual general meeting is held. Where no AGM is held in a year, the sixty days run from the date on which it should have been held.

questions.question_text: Lotus Ltd was incorporated on 15 February of Year 1. By which date must it hold its first annual general meeting under section 96?

options.A: 30 September of Year 1
options.B: 31 December of Year 2
options.C: 31 December of Year 1
options.D: 15 November of Year 1

questions.explanation: Under section 2(41), a company incorporated on or after 1 January has its first financial year ending on 31 March of the following year. Lotus Ltd's first financial year therefore runs from 15 February Year 1 to 31 March Year 2. Section 96(1) requires the first AGM within nine months of the close of the first financial year, which is 31 December Year 2.

questions.question_text: Garnet Ltd held its last AGM on 25 July of Year 1. Its financial year ended on 31 March of Year 2. Ignoring any extension by the Registrar, what is the latest date by which it must hold its next AGM?

options.A: 25 July of Year 2
options.B: 30 September of Year 2
options.C: 31 December of Year 2
options.D: 25 October of Year 2

questions.explanation: Section 96(1) requires a subsequent AGM within six months of the close of the financial year, and not more than fifteen months between two AGMs. Six months from 31 March Year 2 is 30 September Year 2. Fifteen months from 25 July Year 1 is 25 October Year 2. The earlier of the two, 30 September Year 2, is the deadline.

questions.question_text: The paid-up share capital of Opal Ltd carrying voting rights is ₹60 lakh. Some members holding ₹5 lakh of that capital deposit a requisition for an extraordinary general meeting under section 100. The requisition is:

options.A: Not valid, because they hold less than one-tenth of the paid-up voting capital
options.B: Not valid, because only the Tribunal can call an extraordinary general meeting
options.C: Valid, because any member may requisition a meeting
options.D: Valid, because they hold more than one-twentieth of the paid-up voting capital

questions.explanation: Section 100(2)(a) requires the requisitionists of a company with share capital to hold at least one-tenth of the paid-up share capital that carries voting rights on the date of the requisition. One-tenth of ₹60 lakh is ₹6 lakh. A holding of ₹5 lakh is below this, so the Board is not bound to call the meeting.

questions.question_text: Under section 101(1), an annual general meeting may be called at shorter notice than twenty-one clear days if consent in writing or by electronic mode is given by:

options.A: Not less than ninety-five per cent of the members entitled to vote at the meeting
options.B: All the directors of the company
options.C: A majority in number of the members entitled to vote
options.D: Members holding not less than seventy-five per cent of the paid-up share capital

questions.explanation: The proviso to section 101(1) allows an AGM to be called at shorter notice with the consent of not less than ninety-five per cent of the members entitled to vote. For any other general meeting, consent is needed from a majority in number of members entitled to vote who hold at least ninety-five per cent of the paid-up voting capital (or total voting power).

questions.question_text: Unless the articles require a larger number, what is the quorum for a general meeting of a public company with 3,200 members on the date of the meeting?

options.A: Fifteen members personally present
options.B: Five members personally present
options.C: Two members personally present
options.D: Thirty members personally present

questions.explanation: Under section 103(1)(a), the quorum for a public company is five members personally present if members do not exceed 1,000. It is fifteen if members exceed 1,000 but not 5,000, and thirty if members exceed 5,000. With 3,200 members, the quorum is fifteen. A private company needs two members personally present.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about proxies under section 105 is correct?

options.A: A proxy must be a member, and may speak at the meeting
options.B: The proxy instrument may be deposited at any time before the voting begins
options.C: A proxy need not be a member, and the proxy instrument must be deposited not less than forty-eight hours before the meeting
options.D: A proxy may vote on a show of hands as well as on a poll

questions.explanation: Under section 105(1), a member entitled to attend and vote may appoint another person, whether a member or not, as his proxy. A proxy has no right to speak and may vote only on a poll. Under section 105(4), the articles cannot require the proxy instrument to be lodged more than forty-eight hours before the meeting, which is the usual deadline.

questions.question_text: At a general meeting of Coral Ltd, a resolution was proposed as a special resolution after due notice. 3,000 votes were cast in favour, 1,000 against, and 400 members present abstained. The resolution is:

options.A: Not passed, because votes in favour must be more than three times the votes against
options.B: Passed only as an ordinary resolution
options.C: Passed as a special resolution
options.D: Not passed, because votes in favour are less than three-fourths of all members present

questions.explanation: Under section 114(2), a special resolution needs votes cast in favour to be not less than three times the votes cast against, by members entitled and voting in person, by proxy or by postal ballot. Abstentions are ignored. Here 3,000 = 3 x 1,000, which meets the 'not less than three times' test, so the special resolution is passed.

questions.question_text: Under the Companies Act, 2013, special notice under section 115 is required for a resolution to:

options.A: Remove a director before the expiry of his period of office under section 169
options.B: Re-appoint a director retiring by rotation
options.C: Declare a final dividend
options.D: Adopt the financial statements at an annual general meeting

questions.explanation: Special notice is required where the Act or the articles so provide. Notable cases are the removal of a director under section 169(2), and appointing an auditor other than the retiring auditor or providing that the retiring auditor shall not be reappointed under section 140(4). Under section 115, the notice is given to the company at least fourteen days before the meeting.

questions.question_text: Which of the following can be a source of dividend under section 123(1)?

options.A: Securities premium account
options.B: Profits of the current financial year arrived at after providing for depreciation as per Schedule II
options.C: Surplus arising on revaluation of fixed assets
options.D: Unrealised gains on measuring investments at fair value

questions.explanation: Section 123(1) allows dividend out of the current year's profits after depreciation, out of undistributed profits of previous years after depreciation, or both. It may also be paid out of money provided by the Central or State Government under a guarantee. Unrealised and notional gains, revaluation gains and fair value changes are excluded when computing profits. The securities premium account is capital in nature.

questions.question_text: Under section 123(4), the amount of dividend declared, including interim dividend, must be deposited in a separate account with a scheduled bank within:

options.A: Fifteen days from the date of the AGM notice
options.B: Seven days from the date of declaration
options.C: Five days from the date of declaration
options.D: Thirty days from the date of declaration

questions.explanation: Section 123(4) requires the amount of dividend, including interim dividend, to be deposited in a scheduled bank in a separate account within five days from the date of declaration. Payment to shareholders is then made from this account.

questions.question_text: A dividend declared by Sapphire Ltd has not been paid or claimed within thirty days of declaration. Under section 124(1), the unpaid amount must be transferred to the Unpaid Dividend Account within:

options.A: Five days from the expiry of the thirty days
options.B: Thirty days from the expiry of the thirty days
options.C: Ninety days from the date of declaration
options.D: Seven days from the expiry of the thirty days

questions.explanation: Section 124(1) requires a company to transfer the total unpaid or unclaimed dividend to a special account called the Unpaid Dividend Account. The account must be opened in a scheduled bank within seven days from the expiry of the thirty-day period. Under section 124(2), a statement of the unpaid amounts must be placed on the company's website within ninety days of the transfer.

questions.question_text: Under section 124(5), money in the Unpaid Dividend Account that remains unpaid or unclaimed must be transferred, with interest accrued, to the Investor Education and Protection Fund after a period of:

options.A: Five years from the date of transfer to the Unpaid Dividend Account
options.B: Seven years from the date of transfer to the Unpaid Dividend Account
options.C: Ten years from the date of declaration
options.D: Three years from the date of declaration

questions.explanation: Section 124(5) requires any money in the Unpaid Dividend Account that is unpaid or unclaimed for seven years from the date of transfer to be transferred, with interest accrued, to the IEPF established under section 125. Under section 124(6), shares on which dividend has been unpaid or unclaimed for seven consecutive years are also transferred to the IEPF.

questions.question_text: Emerald Ltd declared dividends of 10%, 12% and 8% in the three immediately preceding financial years. It has incurred a loss in the current financial year up to the end of the quarter immediately before the date on which the Board proposes an interim dividend. What is the maximum rate of interim dividend it can declare?

options.C: No interim dividend can be declared

questions.explanation: The proviso to section 123(3) states that where a company has incurred a loss in the current year up to the end of the quarter immediately preceding the declaration, interim dividend cannot exceed the average of the dividends declared in the immediately preceding three financial years. Average = (10 + 12 + 8) / 3 = 30 / 3 = 10%. The loss does not prohibit interim dividend outright.

questions.question_text: Under section 123(6), a company that has failed to comply with the provisions of sections 73 and 74 (acceptance and repayment of deposits) shall not declare dividend on:

options.A: Its equity shares only if the Tribunal so orders
options.B: Any class of shares for five years after the failure
options.C: Its preference shares only
options.D: Its equity shares, so long as the failure continues

questions.explanation: Section 123(6) provides that a company that fails to comply with sections 73 and 74 shall not, so long as the failure continues, declare any dividend on its equity shares. The prohibition protects depositors by stopping profits being paid out while deposits remain in default.

questions.question_text: Under section 127, a director is NOT liable for failure to pay a declared dividend within thirty days in which of the following cases?

options.A: The company decided to use the funds for working capital
options.B: The Board decided to postpone payment until the next quarter
options.C: The bank account of the company had insufficient balance due to other payments
options.D: There is a dispute regarding the right to receive the dividend

questions.explanation: The proviso to section 127 lists cases where no offence is committed. These are: dividend could not be paid because of the operation of law; the shareholder's directions could not be complied with; there is a dispute about the right to receive the dividend; the dividend was lawfully adjusted against a sum due from the shareholder; or the failure was not due to any default of the company. Diverting the funds or lacking money are not excuses.

questions.question_text: Under the fourth proviso to section 123(1), before declaring dividend for the current financial year a company must:

options.A: Redeem all outstanding preference shares
options.B: Transfer at least ten per cent of profits to a general reserve
options.C: Obtain the approval of the Registrar for the rate of dividend
options.D: Set off carried over previous losses and depreciation not provided in previous years against the profit of the current year

questions.explanation: The fourth proviso to section 123(1) requires carried over previous losses and depreciation not provided in previous years to be set off against the current year's profit before any dividend is declared for that year. There is no compulsory transfer to reserves; the company may transfer such percentage of profits as it thinks appropriate.

questions.question_text: Under section 126, where an instrument of transfer of shares has been delivered to the company but the transfer has not yet been registered, the company shall:

options.A: Cancel the dividend on those shares
options.B: Pay the dividend to the transferor immediately
options.C: Pay the dividend to the transferee named in the instrument of transfer
options.D: Transfer the dividend relating to those shares to the Unpaid Dividend Account, unless the registered holder authorises in writing payment to the transferee

questions.explanation: Section 126 provides that where a transfer instrument has been delivered but the transfer is not registered, the company shall transfer the dividend on those shares to the Unpaid Dividend Account under section 124. This applies unless the registered holder authorises the company in writing to pay it to the transferee. Rights and bonus shares on those shares are similarly kept in abeyance.

questions.question_text: Under section 128(5), a company must preserve its books of account, together with relevant vouchers, in good order for a period of not less than:

options.A: Eight financial years immediately preceding a financial year
options.B: Six financial years immediately preceding a financial year
options.C: Ten financial years immediately preceding a financial year
options.D: Five financial years immediately preceding a financial year

questions.explanation: Section 128(5) requires the books of account of every company relating to a period of not less than eight financial years immediately preceding a financial year to be kept in good order. Where an investigation has been ordered, the Central Government may direct that they be kept for a longer period.

questions.question_text: Under section 128(1), the Board of Rose Ltd decides to keep the books of account at a place in India other than the registered office. The company must:

options.A: Obtain the approval of the Central Government
options.B: Obtain a special resolution of members before shifting the books
options.C: File with the Registrar a notice in writing giving the full address of that place within seven days of the Board's decision
options.D: Keep the books outside the registered office only in electronic form

questions.explanation: The proviso to section 128(1) allows the Board to decide that the books of account be kept at another place in India. The company must file a notice in writing with the Registrar giving the full address of that place within seven days of the decision. The books must be kept on an accrual basis and according to the double entry system.

questions.question_text: Under section 2(40), which of the following companies may exclude the cash flow statement from its financial statements?

options.A: A company that has issued debentures to the public
options.B: A public company with net worth above the threshold under section 135
options.C: A listed company
options.D: A small company

questions.explanation: The proviso to section 2(40) permits a One Person Company, a small company, a dormant company and a private company that is a start-up to omit the cash flow statement. A listed company or a large public company must include it.

questions.question_text: Under section 129(3), a company must prepare consolidated financial statements in addition to its own financial statements where it has:

options.A: Borrowings from banks and financial institutions
options.B: More than two hundred members
options.C: One or more subsidiaries or associate companies
options.D: Branches located outside India

questions.explanation: Section 129(3) requires a company with one or more subsidiaries or associate companies to prepare a consolidated financial statement of the company and all its subsidiaries and associates in the same form and manner as its own. The Explanation clarifies that 'subsidiary' includes associate company and joint venture.

questions.question_text: The directors of Iris Ltd discover that its financial statements for one of the three preceding financial years did not comply with section 129. Under section 131, they may prepare revised financial statements:

options.A: Without any approval, as often as necessary
options.B: Only on an order of the Central Government, for any of the last eight years
options.C: After passing a special resolution, for any earlier financial year
options.D: After obtaining the approval of the Tribunal, and not more than once in a financial year

questions.explanation: Section 131(1) allows directors to prepare revised financial statements or a revised Board's report for any of the three preceding financial years where they do not comply with section 129 or 134. This requires the Tribunal's approval on an application in the prescribed form. The proviso limits revision to once in a financial year. Reopening of accounts on the application of authorities is dealt with separately under section 130.

questions.question_text: Under section 130, the books of account of a company can be reopened and its financial statements recast:

options.A: By a special resolution of members, for any period
options.B: By the Board of directors on discovering any arithmetical error
options.C: Only on an order of the Registrar, for the last three financial years
options.D: Only on an order of a court of competent jurisdiction or the Tribunal, and not for a period earlier than eight financial years immediately preceding the current year

questions.explanation: Section 130(1) allows reopening only on an order of a court or the Tribunal. The application may be made by the Central Government, the income-tax authorities, SEBI, any other statutory regulatory body or any person concerned. It must show that the accounts were prepared fraudulently or that the affairs were mismanaged, casting doubt on the reliability of the statements. Section 130(2) bars reopening for a period earlier than eight financial years preceding the current year.

questions.question_text: As per section 134(1), the financial statements of a company that has a managing director, CFO and company secretary (and no Board-authorised chairperson) must be approved by the Board and signed by:

options.A: The company secretary alone
options.B: Any one director and the statutory auditor
options.C: All the directors and the CFO
options.D: Two directors, one of whom is the managing director, and the CFO and the company secretary

questions.explanation: Section 134(1) requires the financial statements to be approved by the Board before they are signed. They are signed at least by the chairperson, where authorised by the Board, or by two directors of whom one is the managing director, if any. The CEO, CFO and company secretary also sign, wherever appointed. For an OPC, one director signs. The auditor signs his own report, not the statements.

questions.question_text: Verdant Ltd is required to comply with section 135. Its net profits computed under section 198 for the three immediately preceding financial years were ₹12 crore, ₹15 crore and ₹18 crore. What is the minimum CSR expenditure for the current financial year?

options.A: ₹24 lakh
options.B: ₹90 lakh
options.C: ₹30 lakh
options.D: ₹36 lakh

questions.explanation: Section 135(5) requires the Board to ensure that the company spends at least two per cent of its average net profits made during the three immediately preceding financial years. Average = (12 + 15 + 18) / 3 = ₹15 crore. CSR obligation = 2% x ₹15 crore = ₹0.30 crore = ₹30 lakh. Using only the latest year's profit would give ₹36 lakh, which is wrong.

questions.question_text: Under section 137(1), a company must file a copy of its adopted financial statements with the Registrar within:

options.A: Seven days of the date of the Board meeting
options.B: Six months from the close of the financial year
options.C: Thirty days of the date of the annual general meeting
options.D: Sixty days of the date of the annual general meeting

questions.explanation: Section 137(1) requires a copy of the financial statements, including consolidated statements, adopted at the AGM to be filed with the Registrar within thirty days of the date of the AGM. A One Person Company files within 180 days from the close of the financial year. Note the difference from the annual return, which is filed within sixty days of the AGM.

questions.question_text: Under section 136(1), a copy of the financial statements with the auditor's report must be sent to every member at least ______ before the date of the general meeting at which they are to be laid.

options.A: Seven days
options.B: Thirty days
options.C: Twenty-one days
options.D: Fourteen days

questions.explanation: Section 136(1) requires a copy of the financial statements, including consolidated statements, the auditor's report and every other document required to be attached, to be sent to every member, trustee for debenture-holders and other persons entitled. They must be sent not less than twenty-one days before the meeting. A shorter period is permitted where the AGM is called at shorter notice.

questions.question_text: Under section 139(1), the auditor appointed at the first annual general meeting holds office:

options.A: For a fixed period of three financial years
options.B: Till the conclusion of the next annual general meeting only
options.C: From the conclusion of that meeting till the conclusion of its sixth annual general meeting
options.D: Till the auditor resigns or is removed, without any time limit

questions.explanation: Section 139(1) requires every company, at its first AGM, to appoint an individual or a firm as auditor to hold office from the conclusion of that meeting till the conclusion of its sixth AGM. Thereafter, the same applies at every sixth meeting. The auditor's written consent and eligibility certificate must be obtained, and the company must inform the Registrar.

questions.question_text: An audit firm has been the auditor of Vertex Ltd, a listed company, for two consecutive terms of five years each. Under section 139(2), the firm:

options.A: Can never again be appointed as auditor of Vertex Ltd
options.B: Cannot be reappointed as auditor of Vertex Ltd for five years from the completion of its second term
options.C: Can be reappointed immediately for one more term of five years by special resolution
options.D: Can be reappointed after a cooling-off period of three years

questions.explanation: Section 139(2)(b) prohibits a listed company, and other prescribed companies, from appointing an audit firm for more than two terms of five consecutive years. The firm is not eligible for reappointment for five years from the completion of its term. An individual auditor is limited to one term of five consecutive years, with the same five-year cooling-off period.

questions.question_text: Fern Ltd is a non-government company. Under section 139(6), its first auditor must be appointed by the Board within thirty days of registration. If the Board fails to do so, the members must appoint the first auditor:

options.A: Within ninety days at an extraordinary general meeting
options.B: Within thirty days at an extraordinary general meeting
options.C: At the first annual general meeting
options.D: Within sixty days, after the Comptroller and Auditor-General is consulted

questions.explanation: Under section 139(6), the first auditor of a non-government company is appointed by the Board within thirty days of registration. If the Board fails, it must inform the members, who appoint the auditor within ninety days at an extraordinary general meeting. The first auditor holds office till the conclusion of the first AGM.

questions.question_text: The auditor of Willow Ltd (not audited by the CAG) resigned mid-term. Under section 139(8), the casual vacancy:

options.A: Is filled by the Registrar within thirty days
options.B: Is filled by the Board within thirty days, and the appointment must also be approved by the company at a general meeting convened within three months of the Board's recommendation
options.C: Is filled by the Board, and no approval of members is required
options.D: Must be filled by members at the next AGM only

questions.explanation: Section 139(8)(i) provides that a casual vacancy in a company not audited by the CAG is filled by the Board within thirty days. If the vacancy arises from the auditor's resignation, the appointment must also be approved by the company at a general meeting convened within three months of the Board's recommendation. The auditor holds office till the conclusion of the next AGM.

questions.question_text: Under section 140(1), an auditor appointed under section 139 may be removed from office before the expiry of his term only by:

options.A: An order of the Registrar on a complaint by members
options.B: An ordinary resolution of the company passed with special notice
options.C: A resolution of the Board of directors
options.D: A special resolution of the company, after obtaining the previous approval of the Central Government

questions.explanation: Section 140(1) requires a special resolution of the company after obtaining the previous approval of the Central Government before an auditor can be removed during his term. The auditor must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard. Removing an auditor at the end of the term, by not reappointing him, needs special notice under section 140(4).

questions.question_text: Which of the following is eligible for appointment as auditor of a company under section 141?

options.A: A private company whose directors are all chartered accountants
options.B: A chartered accountant who is in full-time employment with another company
options.C: A chartered accountant who is a full-time employee of the company
options.D: A limited liability partnership registered under the LLP Act, 2008, in which the partners who sign are chartered accountants

questions.explanation: Section 141(1) allows a firm, including an LLP, to be appointed by its name if a majority of its partners practising in India are qualified; only chartered accountant partners may act and sign. Section 141(3)(a) disqualifies a body corporate other than an LLP. An officer or employee of the company, and a person in full-time employment elsewhere, are disqualified under section 141(3)(b) and (g).

questions.question_text: Under section 141(3)(g), a chartered accountant is disqualified from being appointed auditor of a company if, at the date of appointment, he is:

options.A: Holding a certificate of practice for less than five years
options.B: Holding appointment as auditor of more than twenty companies, counted as provided in that clause
options.C: Auditor of any other company in the same industry
options.D: Holding appointment as auditor of more than ten companies of any kind

questions.explanation: Section 141(3)(g) disqualifies a person who is in full-time employment elsewhere, or a person or partner of a firm who already holds appointment as auditor of more than twenty companies. Certain categories of companies are excluded from this count by the clause. There is no prohibition on auditing competitors, and no minimum years of practice under the Act.

questions.question_text: Under section 144, which of the following services can a company's statutory auditor provide to it, with approval of the Board or audit committee?

options.A: Representation of the company in income-tax assessment proceedings
options.B: Investment advisory services
options.C: Internal audit
options.D: Design and implementation of a financial information system

questions.explanation: Section 144 lists services an auditor cannot provide directly or indirectly to the company, its holding company or subsidiary. These are accounting and book-keeping, internal audit, design and implementation of financial information systems, actuarial services, investment advisory, investment banking, outsourced financial services, management services and other prescribed services. Taxation representation is not in the list, so it is permitted with the approval of the Board or audit committee.

questions.question_text: Under section 143(1), the auditor of a company has the right of access to the books of account and vouchers of the company:

options.A: Only on giving seven days' written notice to the company
options.B: At all times, whether kept at the registered office or elsewhere
options.C: Only with the permission of the Board
options.D: Only during the period of the statutory audit

questions.explanation: Section 143(1) gives every auditor a right of access at all times to the books of account and vouchers of the company, wherever kept. The auditor may also require from the officers such information and explanations as he considers necessary for his duties.

questions.question_text: Under section 148(3), which of the following persons cannot be appointed to conduct the cost audit of a company?

options.A: The statutory auditor of the company appointed under section 139
options.B: A cost accountant in practice who is not otherwise disqualified
options.C: A cost accountant who audited the cost records of the company in the previous year
options.D: A firm of cost accountants

questions.explanation: Section 148(3) requires the cost audit to be conducted by a cost accountant appointed by the Board. It expressly provides that no person appointed under section 139 as the company's auditor shall be appointed to audit its cost records. This keeps the financial and cost audits independent.

questions.question_text: During the audit of Maple Ltd, the auditor has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving an amount above the threshold prescribed under section 143(12) is being committed by its employees. The auditor must report the matter to:

options.A: The Registrar of Companies only
options.B: The Central Government, within the prescribed time and manner
options.C: The police, with a copy to the Board
options.D: The members at the next annual general meeting only

questions.explanation: Section 143(12) requires an auditor who has reason to believe that an offence of fraud is being or has been committed by the company's officers or employees to report it. For fraud above the prescribed amount, the report goes to the Central Government. Smaller frauds are reported to the audit committee or Board and disclosed in the Board's report.

questions.question_text: Under section 2(42), which of the following is a 'foreign company'?

options.A: A company incorporated outside India that has a place of business in India, whether by itself, through an agent, physically or through electronic mode, and conducts business activity in India
options.B: A company incorporated in India that has a branch outside India
options.C: Any company listed on a stock exchange outside India
options.D: A company incorporated in India whose shares are held entirely by foreign nationals

questions.explanation: Section 2(42) defines a foreign company as a company or body corporate incorporated outside India which has a place of business in India by itself or through an agent, physically or through electronic mode, and conducts any business activity in India in any other manner. A company incorporated in India is never a foreign company, regardless of who owns its shares.

questions.question_text: Under section 379, a foreign company must comply with Chapter XXII and other prescribed provisions as if it were a company incorporated in India where:

options.A: Not less than fifty per cent of its paid-up share capital is held by one or more citizens of India or companies or bodies corporate incorporated in India
options.B: Its turnover from business in India exceeds its turnover outside India
options.C: More than twenty-five per cent of its directors are citizens of India
options.D: Its principal place of business is in India

questions.explanation: Section 379 applies where not less than fifty per cent of the paid-up share capital (equity, preference or both) of a foreign company is held by citizens of India and/or companies or bodies corporate incorporated in India, singly or in aggregate. Such a company must then comply with the Chapter and other prescribed provisions for its business in India as if it were an Indian company.

questions.question_text: Under section 380(1), a foreign company must deliver the prescribed documents to the Registrar for registration within:

options.A: Six months of commencing business in India
options.B: Thirty days of the close of its first financial year
options.C: Thirty days of the establishment of its place of business in India
options.D: Sixty days of the establishment of its place of business in India

questions.explanation: Section 380(1) requires every foreign company to deliver documents to the Registrar within thirty days of establishing a place of business in India. These include a certified copy of its charter or memorandum and articles, its registered office address, a list of directors and secretary, and details of persons resident in India authorised to accept service. Any alteration must be filed within thirty days under section 380(3).

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a requirement of section 382 for a foreign company?

options.A: It must add the word 'India' to the end of its name
options.B: It must keep its books of account only at its head office outside India
options.C: It must appoint an Indian citizen as its chairman
options.D: It must display its name and the country in which it is incorporated outside every office or place of business in India, in English and in a local language in use

questions.explanation: Section 382 requires every foreign company to conspicuously display, outside every office or place where it carries on business in India, its name and the country of incorporation, in English and in the local language in use there. The name and country must also appear on its business letters, bill-heads and letter paper, and in all notices and official publications. If members' liability is limited, that fact must also be stated.

questions.question_text: A foreign company has not filed the documents required under Chapter XXII. It entered into a supply contract in India and now wishes to sue the buyer for non-payment. Under section 393:

options.A: The contract is valid, but the company cannot bring a suit in respect of it until it complies with the applicable provisions
options.B: The contract is void because of the non-compliance
options.C: The contract becomes voidable at the option of the buyer
options.D: The company can sue freely, since non-compliance only attracts a fine

questions.explanation: Section 393 provides that failure to comply with Chapter XXII does not affect the validity of any contract, dealing or transaction, or the company's liability to be sued. However, the company cannot bring any suit, claim any set-off, make a counter-claim or start any legal proceeding in respect of it until it has complied with the provisions applicable to it.

questions.question_text: For the purposes of Chapter XXII, section 386 provides that the expression 'place of business' includes:
