options.A: Only a registered office of an Indian subsidiary
options.B: Only a manufacturing facility in India
options.C: A share transfer or registration office
options.D: Any place where its goods are sold by independent dealers

questions.explanation: Section 386 states that 'place of business' includes a share transfer or registration office. The same section explains that 'certified' means certified as a true copy in the prescribed manner, and that 'director' includes any person in accordance with whose directions or instructions the Board of the foreign company is accustomed to act.

questions.question_text: Under section 3 of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, a limited liability partnership is:

options.A: A body corporate formed and incorporated under the Act, being a legal entity separate from its partners
options.B: An association of persons with no legal existence apart from its partners
options.C: A company limited by guarantee registered under the Companies Act, 2013
options.D: A firm registered under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 with limited liability

questions.explanation: Section 3(1) provides that an LLP is a body corporate formed and incorporated under the LLP Act and is a legal entity separate from its partners. Section 3(2) gives it perpetual succession, and any change in partners does not affect its existence, rights or liabilities. Section 4 states that the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 does not apply to an LLP.

questions.question_text: Alpha LLP had two partners. One partner died, and the LLP continued its business with only the surviving partner for nine months. Under section 6(2), the surviving partner, who knew of the situation, is:

options.A: Not personally liable, as an LLP partner's liability is always limited
options.B: Personally liable for all obligations of the LLP since its incorporation
options.C: Liable only to the extent of his agreed contribution
options.D: Personally liable for the obligations of the LLP incurred during the period after the first six months

questions.explanation: Section 6(1) requires every LLP to have at least two partners. Under section 6(2), if the number falls below two and the LLP carries on business for more than six months while so reduced, the sole partner who knows of this is personally liable. The liability covers the LLP's obligations incurred during the period after those six months.

questions.question_text: As per section 7(1), every LLP must have at least:

options.A: One designated partner who is resident in India
options.B: Two designated partners who are individuals, at least one of whom is resident in India
options.C: Two designated partners, both of whom must be resident in India
options.D: Two designated partners, who may be bodies corporate

questions.explanation: Section 7(1) requires every LLP to have at least two designated partners who are individuals, at least one of whom must be a resident in India. Where all partners are bodies corporate, or some are individuals and some bodies corporate, individuals or nominees of the bodies corporate act as designated partners.

questions.question_text: Under section 5, which of the following is NOT capable of becoming a partner of an LLP?

options.A: A non-resident individual
options.B: An individual who has been found to be of unsound mind by a court of competent jurisdiction
options.C: A company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013
options.D: An LLP incorporated under the LLP Act, 2008

questions.explanation: Section 5 allows any individual or body corporate to be a partner. An individual is not capable if found by a competent court to be of unsound mind, is an undischarged insolvent, or has applied to be adjudicated insolvent and the application is pending. Companies and LLPs are bodies corporate, and residence is not a condition for being a partner.

questions.question_text: In the absence of an LLP agreement on the matter, the First Schedule to the LLP Act provides that the partners shall share the capital, profits and losses of the LLP:

options.A: Equally
options.B: In the ratio of their contributions
options.C: In the ratio decided by the designated partners
options.D: In the ratio of the time devoted to the business

questions.explanation: Under section 23(4), where no LLP agreement exists or it is silent on a matter, the First Schedule applies. Paragraph 1 of the First Schedule provides that the mutual rights and duties of the partners are determined so that all partners are entitled to share equally in the capital, profits and losses of the LLP.

questions.question_text: Unless the LLP agreement provides otherwise, which of the following is correct under the First Schedule?

options.A: No person may be introduced as a partner without the consent of all the existing partners
options.B: Every partner is entitled to remuneration for acting in the business
options.C: A majority of partners may expel any partner without a power in the agreement
options.D: A change in the nature of business can be made by a simple majority of partners

questions.explanation: The First Schedule provides that no person may be introduced as a partner without the consent of all existing partners. No partner is entitled to remuneration for acting in the business. No majority may expel a partner unless the agreement expressly gives that power. Ordinary matters are decided by a majority, but a change in the nature of business needs the consent of all partners.

questions.question_text: In the absence of any agreement with the other partners, under section 24(1) a partner may cease to be a partner of an LLP by giving a notice in writing to the other partners of not less than:

options.A: Fifteen days
options.B: Ninety days
options.C: Thirty days
options.D: Sixty days

questions.explanation: Section 24(1) states that a person may cease to be a partner in accordance with an agreement with the other partners. In the absence of an agreement, he may do so by giving a notice in writing of not less than thirty days to the other partners of his intention to resign. A person also ceases to be a partner on death, dissolution of the LLP, or on being declared of unsound mind or insolvent.

questions.question_text: Partner P of Beta LLP negligently caused a loss to a client while acting in the course of the LLP's business. Partner Q had no role in it. Under sections 27 and 28, which is correct?

options.A: Only Beta LLP is liable, and P cannot be made personally liable
options.B: Only P is liable; the LLP is not liable for acts of its partners
options.C: Beta LLP is liable to the client, P is personally liable for his own wrongful act, and Q is not personally liable merely because he is a partner
options.D: Beta LLP, P and Q are all jointly and severally liable without limit

questions.explanation: Under section 27(2), an LLP is liable if a partner is liable to any person as a result of a wrongful act or omission in the course of the LLP's business or with its authority. Section 28(1) provides that a partner is not personally liable for an obligation of the LLP solely because he is a partner. Section 28(2) preserves a partner's personal liability for his own wrongful act or omission.

questions.question_text: Under section 30, where an act is carried out by an LLP or any of its partners with intent to defraud its creditors:

options.A: Only the LLP is liable, up to the value of its assets
options.B: All partners become liable without limit, whether or not they took part in the fraud
options.C: The liability of the LLP and of the partners who acted with that intent is unlimited for all or any of the debts or liabilities of the LLP
options.D: The partners who acted with that intent are liable only up to their contribution

questions.explanation: Section 30(1) provides that where an act is carried out with intent to defraud creditors or for any fraudulent purpose, the liability of the LLP and of the partners who acted with that intent is unlimited for all or any of the LLP's debts. Partners who were not involved are not made liable without limit. Section 30(2) also provides punishment for those who were knowingly parties to the act.

questions.question_text: Under section 34(2), every LLP must prepare a Statement of Account and Solvency for each financial year within:

options.A: Six months from the end of the financial year
options.B: Nine months from the end of the financial year
options.C: Thirty days from the end of the financial year
options.D: Sixty days from the end of the financial year

questions.explanation: Section 34(2) requires every LLP to prepare a Statement of Account and Solvency within six months from the end of each financial year. It must be signed by the designated partners and filed with the Registrar. The annual return under section 35 is filed within sixty days of the close of the financial year.

questions.question_text: Under section 56 read with the Third Schedule, a private company may apply to convert into an LLP only if:

options.A: At least seventy-five per cent of its shareholders agree to become partners of the LLP
options.B: There is no security interest in its assets subsisting or in force at the time of application, and the partners of the LLP will comprise all the shareholders of the company and no one else
options.C: It has obtained the approval of the Tribunal and its creditors
options.D: It has been in existence for at least five years

questions.explanation: The Third Schedule permits a private company to convert into an LLP only where there is no security interest in its assets subsisting or in force at the time of application. The partners of the LLP must comprise all the shareholders of the company and no one else. On conversion, the company's property, rights and liabilities vest in the LLP and the company is deemed dissolved.

questions.topic: The General Clauses Act, 1897 and Interpretation of Statutes
questions.question_text: Under section 3(42) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, the term 'person' includes:

options.A: Any company or association or body of individuals, whether incorporated or not
options.B: Only individuals and companies registered under the Companies Act
options.C: Only natural persons who have attained majority
options.D: Only bodies incorporated under a Central Act

questions.explanation: Section 3(42) of the General Clauses Act provides that 'person' shall include any company or association or body of individuals, whether incorporated or not. This wide definition applies in all Central Acts and Regulations unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context.

questions.topic: The General Clauses Act, 1897 and Interpretation of Statutes
questions.question_text: Under section 3(22) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, a thing is deemed to be done in 'good faith' where it is in fact done:

options.A: With due care and attention
options.B: In accordance with the advice of an expert
options.C: Honestly and without any negligence
options.D: Honestly, whether it is done negligently or not

questions.explanation: Section 3(22) provides that a thing shall be deemed to be done in good faith where it is in fact done honestly, whether it is done negligently or not. The test is honesty, not carefulness. This contrasts with the Indian Penal Code, where good faith requires due care and attention.

questions.topic: The General Clauses Act, 1897 and Interpretation of Statutes
questions.question_text: A notification grants a concession for goods imported 'from 1 March to 10 March'. Applying section 9 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, the concession covers:

options.A: Goods imported on 1 March to 9 March, both days inclusive (nine days)
options.B: Goods imported on 1 March to 10 March, both days inclusive (ten days)
options.C: Goods imported on 2 March to 10 March, both days inclusive (nine days)
options.D: Goods imported on 2 March to 9 March, both days inclusive (eight days)

questions.explanation: Section 9 provides that the word 'from' is used to exclude the first in a series of days, and the word 'to' is used to include the last. So 1 March is excluded and 10 March is included. The concession covers 2 March to 10 March, which is 10 - 2 + 1 = 9 days.

questions.topic: The General Clauses Act, 1897 and Interpretation of Statutes
questions.question_text: An Act under which a prosecution had already started is repealed by a new Act. The repealing Act shows no different intention. Under section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897:

options.A: The pending prosecution may be continued and any penalty imposed as if the repealing Act had not been passed
options.B: The prosecution abates automatically on the date of repeal
options.C: The prosecution may continue only if the repealing Act expressly saves it
options.D: The prosecution must be restarted under the new Act

questions.explanation: Section 6 provides that, unless a different intention appears, the repeal of an enactment does not affect any investigation, legal proceeding or remedy regarding any right, liability, penalty or punishment incurred under it. Such proceedings may be instituted, continued or enforced as if the repealing Act had not been passed. Repeal also does not revive anything not in force when the repeal takes effect.

questions.topic: The General Clauses Act, 1897 and Interpretation of Statutes
questions.question_text: Under section 26 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, where an act or omission is an offence under two or more enactments, the offender:

options.A: Can be prosecuted only under the enactment passed first
options.B: Can be prosecuted only under the enactment with the lesser punishment
options.C: Is liable to be prosecuted and punished under either or any of them, but not punished twice for the same offence
options.D: Must be prosecuted and punished under all the enactments

questions.explanation: Section 26 provides that where an act or omission constitutes an offence under two or more enactments, the offender is liable to be prosecuted and punished under either or any of them. He shall not be liable to be punished twice for the same offence, reflecting the rule against double jeopardy.

questions.topic: The General Clauses Act, 1897 and Interpretation of Statutes
questions.question_text: Under section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, where a Central Act requires a document to be served by post, service is deemed to be effected by:

options.A: Sending the document by ordinary post, at the time of posting
options.B: Handing over the document personally to the addressee only
options.C: Properly addressing, pre-paying and posting by registered post a letter containing the document, at the time it would be delivered in the ordinary course of post
options.D: Publishing the document in the Official Gazette

questions.explanation: Section 27 provides that, unless a different intention appears, service by post is deemed effected by properly addressing, pre-paying and posting by registered post a letter containing the document. Unless the contrary is proved, service is deemed made at the time the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post.

questions.topic: The General Clauses Act, 1897 and Interpretation of Statutes
questions.question_text: Which rule of interpretation is regarded as the primary rule, requiring the words of a statute to be given their plain and ordinary meaning when they are clear and unambiguous?

options.A: The rule of beneficial construction
options.B: The rule of harmonious construction
options.C: The mischief rule
options.D: The literal rule

questions.explanation: The literal rule is the primary rule of interpretation. Where the language of a statute is plain and unambiguous, the court must give effect to it whatever the consequences, because the legislature is presumed to mean what it says. Other rules are used mainly when the words are ambiguous or lead to absurdity.

questions.topic: The General Clauses Act, 1897 and Interpretation of Statutes
questions.question_text: The mischief rule of interpretation, laid down in Heydon's case, requires the court to consider four matters. Which of the following is NOT one of them?

options.A: What was the mischief and defect for which the common law did not provide
options.B: The views of the Minister who moved the Bill, as recorded in a newspaper
options.C: What remedy Parliament resolved to provide, and the true reason for the remedy
options.D: What was the common law before the making of the Act

questions.explanation: Heydon's case (1584) asks the court to consider: the common law before the Act; the mischief and defect for which the common law did not provide; the remedy Parliament resolved to provide; and the true reason for the remedy. The court then adopts the construction that suppresses the mischief and advances the remedy. Newspaper reports of a Minister's views are not part of the test.

questions.topic: The General Clauses Act, 1897 and Interpretation of Statutes
questions.question_text: A statute imposes a licence fee on 'cars, buses, lorries, vans and other vehicles'. Applying the rule of ejusdem generis, the words 'other vehicles' would most likely be read to include:

options.A: Every means of transport of any kind
options.B: Aircraft and ships
options.C: Bicycles and handcarts
options.D: Motorised road vehicles similar to those listed

questions.explanation: Under the ejusdem generis rule, where general words follow specific words that form a distinct class or genus, the general words are limited to things of the same class. Cars, buses, lorries and vans form a class of motorised road vehicles. 'Other vehicles' is therefore read as other motorised road vehicles, not bicycles, aircraft or ships.

questions.topic: The General Clauses Act, 1897 and Interpretation of Statutes
questions.question_text: The rule of interpretation under which the meaning of a doubtful word may be ascertained by reference to the meaning of words associated with it is known as:

options.A: Reddendo singula singulis
options.B: Expressio unius est exclusio alterius
options.C: Noscitur a sociis
options.D: Contemporanea expositio

questions.explanation: Noscitur a sociis means 'a word is known by the company it keeps'. Where a word is capable of more than one meaning, its meaning is taken from the words with which it is associated. Ejusdem generis is a particular application of this broader rule.

questions.topic: The General Clauses Act, 1897 and Interpretation of Statutes
questions.question_text: Which of the following is an EXTERNAL aid to the interpretation of a statute?

options.A: An illustration appended to a section of the Act
options.B: Parliamentary history, such as the statement of objects and reasons of the Bill
options.C: A proviso to a section of the Act
options.D: The preamble of the Act

questions.explanation: Internal aids are found within the statute itself, such as the long title, preamble, headings, marginal notes, definitions, provisos, illustrations, explanations and schedules. External aids lie outside the statute and include parliamentary history (such as the statement of objects and reasons and debates), historical facts, dictionaries, statutes in pari materia and judicial decisions.

questions.topic: The General Clauses Act, 1897 and Interpretation of Statutes
questions.question_text: Two sections of the same Act appear to conflict with each other. The court interprets them so that both are given effect as far as possible, without making either of them redundant. This is the rule of:

options.A: Harmonious construction
options.B: Strict construction of penal statutes
options.C: Literal construction
options.D: Exceptional construction

questions.explanation: Under the rule of harmonious construction, provisions of a statute that appear to conflict must be read together and reconciled so that effect is given to both, as far as possible. The court avoids a reading that would make one provision a dead letter, because the legislature is presumed not to have intended an inconsistency.

questions.question_text: The Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 was enacted to consolidate and amend the law relating to foreign exchange with the objective of:

options.A: Conserving foreign exchange by prohibiting all foreign exchange transactions
options.B: Facilitating external trade and payments and promoting the orderly development and maintenance of the foreign exchange market in India
options.C: Prescribing the procedure for levy of customs duty on imports
options.D: Regulating the issue of securities by companies to the public

questions.explanation: The preamble of FEMA states that it is an Act to consolidate and amend the law relating to foreign exchange, with the objective of facilitating external trade and payments and promoting the orderly development and maintenance of the foreign exchange market in India. It replaced the more restrictive Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973.

questions.question_text: Mr. Kunal stayed in India for 250 days during the preceding financial year. In May of the current financial year he left India to take up employment in Dubai. His residential status under section 2(v) of FEMA from the date of his departure is:

options.A: Person resident in India for the whole current financial year, since he stayed more than 182 days in the preceding year
options.B: Person resident in India, since residential status changes only from the next financial year
options.C: Person resident in India until he has stayed abroad for 182 days
options.D: Person resident outside India, as a person who goes out of India for taking up employment outside India is excluded

questions.explanation: Under section 2(v)(i), a person residing in India for more than 182 days in the preceding financial year is resident, but this excludes a person who has gone out of India for or on taking up employment outside India. The exclusion applies from the time he leaves. So Mr. Kunal becomes a person resident outside India from his departure, even though he stayed 250 days in the preceding year.

questions.question_text: Ms. Laura, a foreign national, came to India purely on a long holiday and stayed for 200 days during the preceding financial year. She has no employment or business in India and no intention to stay for an uncertain period. Under section 2(v) of FEMA, she is:

options.A: A person resident in India if the Reserve Bank of India so certifies
options.B: A person resident in India only for the period of her stay
options.C: A person resident in India, because she stayed more than 182 days in the preceding financial year
options.D: A person resident outside India, because she came to India for a purpose other than employment, business or vocation, or an intention to stay for an uncertain period

questions.explanation: Section 2(v)(i)(B) excludes from 'person resident in India' a person who has come to or stays in India otherwise than for employment, for carrying on business or vocation, or for any other purpose indicating an intention to stay for an uncertain period. A stay for a holiday falls within this exclusion. Despite 200 days in the preceding year, she is a person resident outside India.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a current account transaction under section 2(j) of FEMA?

options.A: Remittance by a resident for the living expenses of his parents residing abroad
options.B: Investment by a person resident in India in shares of a foreign company
options.C: Purchase of a residential flat in London by a person resident in India
options.D: Taking a long-term loan from a bank outside India by an Indian company

questions.explanation: Section 2(j) defines a current account transaction as one other than a capital account transaction. It includes payments in connection with foreign trade and services, interest on loans, net income from investments, and remittances for living expenses of parents, spouse and children residing abroad. Acquiring foreign property, foreign shares or long-term foreign borrowing alters assets or liabilities outside India and is a capital account transaction under section 2(e).

questions.question_text: Under section 2(e) of FEMA, a 'capital account transaction' means a transaction which alters:

options.A: Only the foreign currency balances held by authorised dealers
options.B: Only the exports and imports of goods and services of India
options.C: The assets or liabilities, including contingent liabilities, outside India of persons resident in India, or the assets or liabilities in India of persons resident outside India
options.D: Only the current income and expenditure of persons resident in India

questions.explanation: Section 2(e) defines a capital account transaction as one that alters the assets or liabilities, including contingent liabilities, outside India of persons resident in India, or in India of persons resident outside India. It includes the transactions referred to in section 6(3). Payments for trade, services and income are current account transactions.

questions.question_text: Under section 2(n) of FEMA, 'foreign exchange' includes:

options.A: Drafts, travellers' cheques, letters of credit or bills of exchange expressed or drawn in Indian currency but payable in any foreign currency
options.B: Indian currency notes held by a person resident outside India
options.C: Special bank notes issued under section 28A of the RBI Act, 1934
options.D: Gold jewellery held by a person resident in India

questions.explanation: Section 2(n) defines foreign exchange as foreign currency, including deposits, credits and balances payable in foreign currency. It also covers drafts, travellers' cheques, letters of credit or bills of exchange expressed or drawn in Indian currency but payable in foreign currency, and similar instruments drawn by banks outside India payable in Indian currency. Special bank notes are expressly excluded from 'Indian currency' by section 2(q). Gold is not foreign exchange.

questions.question_text: Under section 2(c) of FEMA, an 'authorised person' means:

options.A: Any scheduled commercial bank, whether or not authorised by the RBI
options.B: An authorised dealer, money changer, off-shore banking unit or any other person for the time being authorised under section 10(1) to deal in foreign exchange or foreign securities
options.C: Any person holding a valid passport and visa
options.D: Any exporter registered with the Director General of Foreign Trade

questions.explanation: Section 2(c) defines an authorised person as an authorised dealer, money changer, off-shore banking unit or any other person for the time being authorised under section 10(1) to deal in foreign exchange or foreign securities. Authorisation is given by the Reserve Bank of India on an application under section 10.

questions.question_text: Mr. Sen, a person resident in India, owns a house in Singapore that he inherited from his uncle, who was a person resident outside India. Under section 6(4) of FEMA, Mr. Sen:

options.A: May hold the house but cannot transfer it to anyone
options.B: Must sell the house and repatriate the proceeds within 180 days
options.C: May hold, own, transfer or invest in the house, since it was inherited from a person resident outside India
options.D: May hold the house only with the specific prior approval of the RBI

questions.explanation: Section 6(4) permits a person resident in India to hold, own, transfer or invest in foreign currency, foreign security or immovable property situated outside India if it was acquired, held or owned by him when he was resident outside India, or inherited from a person who was resident outside India. Inherited property therefore needs no further permission.

questions.question_text: A person contravenes a provision of FEMA, and the sum involved in the contravention is quantifiable at ₹4 lakh. Under section 13(1), the maximum penalty that can be imposed (ignoring any continuing contravention) is:

options.A: ₹8 lakh
options.B: ₹12 lakh
options.C: ₹4 lakh
options.D: ₹2 lakh

questions.explanation: Section 13(1) provides for a penalty of up to thrice the sum involved where the amount is quantifiable, or up to ₹2 lakh where it is not quantifiable. A continuing contravention attracts a further penalty of up to ₹5,000 per day after the first day. Maximum = 3 x ₹4 lakh = ₹12 lakh.

questions.question_text: Under section 8 of FEMA, where any amount of foreign exchange is due or has accrued to a person resident in India, that person shall:

options.A: Invest it in foreign securities within ninety days
options.B: Convert it into gold and bring it into India
options.C: Take all reasonable steps to realise and repatriate it to India within the period and manner specified by the RBI
options.D: Hold it outside India indefinitely at his option

questions.explanation: Section 8 provides that, save as otherwise provided, a person resident in India to whom any amount of foreign exchange is due or has accrued must take all reasonable steps to realise and repatriate it to India. This must be done within the period and in the manner specified by the Reserve Bank. Section 9 lists exemptions, such as possession of foreign currency or coins within limits specified by the Reserve Bank.
